name: drop_in_place
documentation:
Executes the destructor (if any) of the pointed-to value.

 See [`ptr::drop_in_place`] for safety concerns and examples.

 [`ptr::drop_in_place`]: crate::ptr::drop_in_place()
rules: `self` must be properly aligned, even if `T` has size 0.
`self` must be nonnull, even if `T` has size 0.
The value pointed to by `self` must be valid for dropping, including any additional invariants required by its type.
While `self.drop_in_place()` is executing, parts of the value pointed to by `self` may be accessed only through the `&mut self` references supplied to the `Drop::drop` methods it invokes.

If `T` is not `Copy`, using the pointed-to value after calling `self.drop_in_place()` can cause undefined behavior; assignment through `*self = foo` counts as such a use because it drops the value again.

After calling `self.drop_in_place()`, `ptr::write` may be used to overwrite the pointed-to storage without dropping the old value, provided the destination remains valid for writes and properly aligned, even for a zero-sized `T`.
`drop_in_place` must be used to drop unsized types, such as trait objects, which cannot be read onto the stack and dropped normally.
`self.drop_in_place()` may be used to drop pinned data when `T` is not `repr(packed)`.
Pinned data must not be moved before it is dropped.
Unaligned values cannot be dropped in place; they must first be copied to an aligned location using `ptr::read_unaligned`. For fields of packed structs, the compiler performs this move automatically.
